h1: Leasing brewery equipment versus buying it outright
title: Leasing Brewery Equipment or Buying It | Craft Beer School
desc: How equipment leases, hire purchase and loans compare with buying a brewhouse outright in India, plus the questions to ask before you sign anything.
teaser: Paying cash for a brewhouse feels safe. It can also leave you with shiny tanks and no money to run them.
standfirst: The equipment decision is really a cash decision. Here is how leasing, hire purchase, loans and outright purchase differ for an Indian brewery and how to compare them on the same page.
sections:
A brewhouse, fermenters, a glycol chiller and a cold room are the biggest cheque most founders ever write. The temptation is to pay it all up front and own everything on day one. The risk is what comes next: licences that take longer than planned, staff on payroll before the first sale and a launch month that needs working capital you no longer have.

Leasing and financing spread the cost of the kit over the years it earns money. Buying outright removes interest and monthly obligations. Neither is right by default. The answer depends on how much cash you have after the equipment is paid for.

• Outright purchase. You pay the supplier, you own the asset and you carry its depreciation on your books. No interest, no lender, no monthly bill.
  • Term loan. A bank or lender funds the purchase, you own the equipment and repay with interest. The equipment often serves as security.
  • Hire purchase. You pay instalments and ownership passes to you after the last one. Until then the financier owns it.
  • Finance lease. You use the kit for most of its working life and pay rentals. Ownership may or may not transfer at the end, depending on the contract.
  • Operating lease or rental. Shorter term, the lessor keeps ownership and the risk of the asset. Common for vehicles, forklifts, generators and some packaging kit, rare for a custom brewhouse.

In India, the lenders active here include banks, non-banking finance companies and sometimes the equipment supplier's own finance partner. Government backed credit guarantee schemes for small enterprises exist and change over time, so ask your bank what currently applies.
Why brewhouses are hard to lease

A lessor wants an asset it could take back and sell. A forklift or a generator has a wide resale market. A 10 hl brewhouse built to fit your basement does not. Expect lenders to want security, a business plan and personal guarantees for brewing equipment. Expect better terms on standard items such as chillers, kegs and canning kit.

Imported equipment adds another layer. Customs duty, freight and installation are often paid in cash before anything is commissioned. A lender may fund only part of the landed cost. Our brewery equipment buying guide covers what to check on the kit itself.
Compare them on the same page

Build a simple sheet that shows, month by month for five years, the cash going out under each option: down payment, instalments or rentals, interest, insurance and maintenance. Then add the tax view your accountant gives you, since depreciation, interest and lease rentals are treated differently and GST may apply to rentals. Only then compare.

Look hardest at the first eighteen months. That is where most small breweries run short. An option that costs more in total but keeps an extra few months of payroll in the bank can be the safer one. Our guide to cash flow in a brewery's first year shows why.

Second-hand brewing kit is a real option in India, as early breweries upgrade or close. Used tanks and brewhouses can cost far less than new, but they are almost never financed on the same terms, because a lender cannot easily value them. That usually means cash. Before you buy, have a brewer inspect welds, jackets, valves and the condition of the insulation. Then price in transport, re-installation and new gaskets. A cheap fermenter with a cooling jacket that leaks glycol is not cheap.

Used equipment can still be the smarter path. Paying cash for a sound used brewhouse and financing new fermenters can leave more working capital than financing everything new. Run it through the same five year cash sheet as every other option.
Questions to ask before you sign

1. What is the effective annual cost, including processing fees and any balloon payment at the end?
  2. Can I prepay? What does it cost?
  3. Who insures the equipment? Who pays for repairs?
  4. What happens if I miss a payment during a licence delay?
  5. Does ownership transfer at the end? At what price?
  6. Can I upgrade or add tanks partway through?

Get the answers in writing. Run the contract past a lawyer and your chartered accountant. These are financial products with legal terms. The details matter more than the brochure.

Many founders end up with a mix. They buy the brewhouse and the core fermenters with equity or a term loan, then lease or finance the items that are easy to value and easy to replace. Kegs, a canning line, a delivery vehicle and a backup generator are typical candidates. That keeps cash for the months when sales are slower than the plan.

Whatever you choose, the decision only makes sense inside a full financial model: capex, working capital, pricing and the realistic ramp-up of sales. That model is the part most founders skip.
faqs: Can I lease a complete brewhouse in India?
It is possible but less common than leasing standard equipment, because a custom brewhouse is hard for a lessor to resell. Expect lenders to ask for security and a detailed plan.
Usually not in total cost, because the lessor earns a return. Its value is in keeping cash free during the early months.
Who should review an equipment lease?
A lawyer for the contract terms and a chartered accountant for the tax and accounting treatment. This guide is not financial or legal advice.
